title: Most biological complexity comes from randomly chosen programs, not natural selection

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Most biological complexity comes from randomly chosen programs, not natural selection

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Most of the complexity seen in biological organisms originates from the abstract fact that many randomly chosen programs produce complex behavior, rather than from adaptation or careful optimization by natural selection.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the vast majority of the complexity we see in biological systems actually has its origin in the purely abstract fact that among randomly chosen programs many give rise to complex behavior.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 8, “Implications for Everyday Systems”; section “Fundamental Issues in Biology” (from p. 383), p. 388. Scope: complex forms and patterns in biological organisms

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch08-11: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.19

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing morphology and phylogeny resources provide outcomes but not the required causal partition. The central reference distribution over programs is undefined, substantially lowering operationalizability. Major new developmental and fitness data would still leave difficult causal-identification assumptions.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Define organismal complexity features, map each to a developmental program, and estimate causal variance attributable to neutral program-output prevalence versus adaptive selection using phylogenetic and fitness data. A dominant neutral-program contribution across a representative feature sample would support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Randomly chosen programs has no natural sampling distribution.

Adaptation and developmental generation are not mutually exclusive causes.

No dataset assigns causal origins to a representative share of biological complexity.

fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.22
data adequacy: 0.1

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Genomes and trees support a proxy comparison between morphological complexity and evidence of selection. That comparison does not isolate an abstract fact about random programs as the source of most biological complexity, because the same patterns are compatible with selection on coarse features. The causal claim is only weakly discriminated by existing data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Relate a complexity score of morphological traits to measures of selection and conservation, and compare the distribution of those traits with the distribution of outputs of short random programs. Complexity concentrated on weakly selected traits, and matching the random-program ensemble, would support the claim; complexity concentrated on strongly selected traits would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Originates from is a historical cause, not a variable stored in sequence or trait databases.

A complex pattern can be both a side effect of a short program and maintained by selection.
